# Retrospective Architecture

This file is the index. The cards live in `resources/`, one file per category.

Choosing starts from the debt the room carries. A routine cadence needs rhythm; a stalled or silent room needs safety before anything else; an incident needs chronology before cause; a launch needs a future before a plan. Read the category that matches the debt, then the one card whose trigger names this room and whose timebox fits the clock.

Keep it blameless. Recite the Prime Directive before the canvas fills, ban counterfactual phrasing in incident work, and treat a broken rule as a signal about the rule rather than a failure of a person. A retro that produces blame produces silence at the next one.

When a room's problem is a workshop exercise rather than a retrospective, the Facilitation Architecture deck is the other shelf. The overlap is deliberate and narrow: TRIZ here (R42) is a retro that names what the team should stop doing; TRIZ there (WS-33) is a workshop that generates deliberately bad ideas about a process. Use this one when the room must commit to stopping; use that one when the room cannot yet name the process.

Rules that hold across every card:

- Recite the Prime Directive before the canvas fills. It arrests hindsight bias; it is not an excuse for the system's faults.
- One canvas, one debt. Do not stack a second ritual onto a room that has not finished the first.
- Anonymous input is a setting, not a courtesy. Use it whenever the trigger names fear, disengagement, restructuring, or an incident.
- A retrospective commits to at most two process experiments. More than that is a wish list that next sprint will not run.
- A finding outside the team's control becomes an adaptation protocol, not a backlog ticket it cannot own.
- Protect the last five minutes. A close that names what the room owes each other is what makes the next retrospective possible.
- An inventory-only card's phases are written for this deck from the method's public definition; the card says so. Do not present them as a source script.

## Foundation & Rhythm (9 cards)

Read `resources/foundation-rhythm.md` for the full card text.

| ID | Card | When to run it |
|---|---|---|
| R01 | Start, Stop, Continue | Operational drift during standard bi-weekly sprint cadences; teams requiring a direct, low-friction mechanism to discard counterproductive habits and institutionalize emerging engineering practices. |
| R02 | Mad, Sad, Glad | Sprints characterized by emotional volatility, interpersonal friction, or organizational friction that technical burndown charts fail to capture. |
| R03 | 4Ls (Loved, Learned, Loathed, Longed For) | Milestone or sprint reviews within engineering teams requiring a balanced evaluation of intellectual growth, product value, and operational friction. |
| R04 | KALM (Keep, Add, Less, More) | Teams experiencing process fatigue that need to modulate the intensity of existing activities rather than reinvent their workflow. |
| R05 | Glad, Sad, Mad + Afraid | Impending corporate reorganizations, high-stakes platform migrations, or strategic pivots where latent psychological anxiety must be addressed directly. |
| R06 | DAKI (Drop, Add, Keep, Improve) | Teams overwhelmed by operational baggage, meeting sprawl, redundant documentation, or outdated tooling. |
| R07 | The Three Little Pigs | Architectural debt retrospectives, stabilization sprints, or infrastructure reviews following high-traffic incidents. |
| R08 | Rose, Thorn, Bud | Product discovery sprints, UI/UX iterations, and collaborative design-engineering syncs. |
| R09 | Plus / Delta (+ / Δ) | High-cadence micro-retrospectives, daily debriefs during release crunches, or rapid 30-minute timeboxed checkpoints. |

## Metaphor & Systems (9 cards)

Read `resources/metaphor-systems.md` for the full card text.

| ID | Card | When to run it |
|---|---|---|
| R10 | The Sailboat | Teams struggling to decouple their aspirational product goals from current technical drag, organizational dependencies, and impending environmental risks. |
| R11 | Speed Car / Race Car | Teams experiencing velocity bottlenecks, deployment throttling, or code review stalls. |
| R12 | Hot Air Balloon | Low-morale sprints where the team needs to acknowledge positive contributions while systematically identifying operational baggage. |
| R13 | Mountain Trek | Multi-sprint delivery campaigns, quarterly releases, or major infrastructural initiatives. |
| R14 | The Hero’s Journey | Post-release reviews following demanding delivery crunches or major technical recoveries. |
| R15 | Space Mission / Rocket | High-risk exploratory initiatives, zero-to-one product development, or deep R&D milestones. |
| R16 | Island Castaway | Sudden loss of team capacity, extreme resource starvation, or emergency operational survival mode. |
| R17 | The Submarine | Accumulated technical debt, creeping memory leaks, latent architectural fragility, or mounting compliance risks. |
| R18 | The Living Tree | Annual retrospectives, long-term engineering health reviews, or major team structural reorganizations. |

## Incident Diagnostics (9 cards)

Read `resources/incident-diagnostics.md` for the full card text.

| ID | Card | When to run it |
|---|---|---|
| R19 | Blameless Post-Mortem Arc | Production service interruptions (SEV-1/SEV-2 outages, data corruption, security breaches). |
| R20 | 5 Whys Fishbone | Chronic, recurring technical defects across sprint cycles that resist simple operational triage. |
| R21 | Swiss Cheese Safety Model | Cascading systemic outages where multiple independent defensive barriers failed simultaneously. |
| R22 | Timeline & Drift Analysis | Operational failures where engineering practices deviated significantly from written operating procedures. |
| R23 | FMEA Diagnostic | Pre-launch architectural reviews, critical database schema migrations, or infrastructure cutovers. |
| R24 | Fault Tree Analysis | Complex microservice outages involving race conditions, deadlocks, or distributed cascading dependencies. |
| R25 | HFACS Retrospective | Incidents characterized by on-call cognitive fatigue, misread alerts, or communication breakdowns during emergency response. |
| R26 | Contributory Factor Matrix | Complex outages cutting across organizational boundaries (e.g., third-party APIs, external vendors, corporate security mandates). |
| R27 | Incident Matrix (4-Box) | Low-severity incidents (SEV-3/SEV-4); recurring bug triage sessions requiring rapid classification. |

Rituals are credited to their public originators where one is documented. The card text, phases and minutes are written for this deck.
